lead: A struct is a value type: assigning it makes a second copy. A class is a reference type: two variables can point at one shared object. Inheritance lets a subclass reuse a superclass and override its methods. Swift uses structs for small model data such as a Trip, and classes for shared state and for UIKit views. Only a few universities teach this topic at this depth. The copy-versus-share rule decides most exam marks, and the override rule decides the rest.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.2 — functions become methods and parameters become initializers.

blocks.text: A struct groups stored properties. struct Trip { var km: Int } gives an automatic memberwise initializer, so Trip(km: 8) is valid without writing an init. The initializer is memberwise: it takes one argument per stored property in declaration order. Assigning a struct copies it. Let a = Trip(km: 8) and var b = a; then set b.km = 12. a.km is still 8 and b.km is 12: two separate copies, not one shared box.

A method that changes a stored property must be marked mutating; without it the compiler stops you. A computed property calculates its value on each read and stores nothing. A didSet observer runs after a stored property changes. String, Array and Dictionary are structs, so they behave as value types when you assign or pass them. For structs that contain arrays or strings, Swift shares the underlying storage until a write; the visible rule is still value semantics.

A class is a reference type. Two variables can point at the same object. class Ride { func fare(km: Int) -> Double { return 20 + Double(km) * 9.0 } } is a base class. class Cab: Ride { override func fare(km: Int) -> Double { return super.fare(km: km) + 15 } } is a subclass. override is required; super.fare calls the parent version. For 8 km, Ride gives 20 + 8 × 9.0 = ₹92 and Cab gives ₹92 + ₹15 = ₹107.

Use === to test whether two class variables point at the same object; == is for value equality. A subclass initializer sets its own stored properties first, then calls super.init. final stops further overriding. deinit runs when the last reference goes away. Polymorphism means a Ride variable can hold a Cab, and the call uses Cab's override.
Choose a struct for small model data that is copied, such as Trip. Choose a class for shared state and for anything UIKit must subclass; see Chapter 6.5.

figure.caption: Calling fare(km: 8) on a Cab first runs Ride's method: 20 + 8 × 9.0 = ₹92.0. The override then adds ₹15, so the Cab returns ₹107.0, while a plain Ride stops at ₹92.0.

examples.question: A bike-taxi app stores a trip as struct Trip { var km: Int }. Start with a = Trip(km: 8), copy it into var b = a, then set b.km = 12. Separately, class Ride has fare(km:) returning 20 + Double(km) * 9.0 rupees; subclass Cab overrides it to add ₹15. Find a.km, b.km, the fare for 8 km by Ride and by Cab. Also state what two variables pointing at one Cab object see if one changes it.
steps: var b = a copies the struct. Setting b.km = 12 leaves a.km = 8 and gives b.km = 12.
Two variables pointing at one Cab object share it, so a change made through one is seen through the other.
examples.answer: a.km = 8, b.km = 12, Ride fare = ₹92.0, Cab fare = ₹107.0; two variables pointing at one Cab object both see a change made through either variable.
examples.check:
km_a = 8
km_b = km_a
km_b = 12
ride = 20 + 8 * 9.0
cab = ride + 15
print(km_a)
print(km_b)
print(ride)
print(cab)

traps: Do not expect var b = a on a struct to share changes back to a; each variable owns a copy.
A subclass method that replaces a superclass method needs override; without it Swift reports a compile error.
A subclass initializer must call super.init after setting its own properties; forgetting it is a compile error.
Use === for class identity, not ==. == asks value equality and may not exist for a class.
A struct method that assigns to a stored property must be mutating.

quiz.q: Which keyword marks a struct method that changes a stored property?
Why does b.km = 12 not change a.km after var b = a for a struct?
quiz.a: Assignment copies the struct, so a and b are separate values.

quiz.q: Ride fare is 20 + km × 9.0 rupees. Cab adds ₹15. Find the fare for 12 km by Ride and by Cab.
Two variables point at the same Cab object. One sets a stored property. What does the other see, and why?
quiz.a: It sees the change because both refer to one shared object (reference semantics).
The subclass is replacing an inherited method with the same signature.

quiz.q: Name two Swift types that are structs.
quiz.a: String and Array; Dictionary is also a struct.

quiz.q: What error appears if a subclass initializer sets its own property but never calls super.init?
quiz.a: A compile error: super.init is not called.

quiz.q: A struct Trip is passed to a function and changed inside. Does the caller's Trip change? Explain.
quiz.a: No; the function receives a copy. To change the caller's value, pass it as inout or return a new value.

beyond: Not for the exam. Swift's protocol-oriented programming often replaces deep class trees with protocols plus structs. Copy-on-write keeps value types cheap: an Array shares a buffer until one copy writes. SwiftUI builds views as structs, while UIKit still relies on class subclassing. Search next: protocol-oriented programming, copy-on-write, value semantics, SwiftUI View struct.
